subsections.heading: 6.3 Measuring persistence and time variation
paragraphs: We measure persistence by the sum of the coefficients on four lags of regional inflation in the regression with time and region fixed effects, estimated with the bias correction of {14} to address the downward bias of autoregressive estimates in panels with short time dimensions. A sum of coefficients close to one indicates highly persistent inflation, and a value near zero indicates that inflation reverts quickly. Persistence is estimated separately for the pre-pandemic period and the post-pandemic period and also from 32-quarter rolling windows.

To let the slope vary smoothly over time, we estimate the baseline equation on rolling windows of 32 quarters and report the slope at the window's end date. Rolling estimates complement the regime comparison, which imposes a break in 2021, by showing whether the change in slope occurred gradually or abruptly, and by allowing us to examine whether the steepening began before the pandemic.

body.heading: 7. Results
paragraphs: We present the main slope estimates, the evolution of the slope over time and the persistence estimates in turn.

subsections.heading: 7.1 The slope of the regional Phillips curve
paragraphs: Table 3 reports the slope estimates by country and period. In the 2010s the instrumented slope was 0.04 (standard error 0.01) in Korea and 0.02 (0.01) in Japan. After 2021 the slopes are 0.09 (0.02) and 0.05 (0.015) respectively. The change is 0.05 in Korea and 0.03 in Japan, and both are significant at the 1 per cent level, supporting H1. In relative terms the slope more than doubles in Korea and rises by a factor of two and a half in Japan, so the curve roughly doubles in both countries. At the same time, the post-pandemic slope in Japan is 0.05 compared with 0.09 in Korea, about 56 per cent of the Korean value, in line with H3 that Japan's curve remains the flatter of the two.

The magnitudes are small in an absolute sense, as in other regional studies [1]. A slope of 0.09 means that a regional labour market that is one percentage point tighter than others has annualised inflation higher by about 0.09 percentage points, so that a three-percentage-point gap in slack between two regions is associated with a difference in annual inflation of roughly a quarter of a percentage point. The relationship is much stronger and more precise than in earlier regional estimates for Japan that relied on ordinary least squares, which we replicate in the first rows of the table: the ordinary least squares slope is 0.02 in Korea and 0.01 in Japan before 2021, and the instrumented slope exceeds them in all cases, consistent with the downward bias from supply shocks and from measurement error in regional slack.

subsections.heading: 7.2 The timing of the steepening
paragraphs: The rolling-window estimates in Figure 1 show that the steepening was gradual rather than abrupt in its early stages but accelerated in 2021 and 2022. Rolling slopes drift up slightly in Korea in 2018 and 2019, a period in which the labour market tightened and minimum wages rose sharply, but they remain close to 0.05 until windows begin to include the post-pandemic observations. The slope then increases quickly, reaching about 0.09 in the window ending 2022 and staying there. In Japan, the slope is stable at about 0.02 until 2020 and rises to 0.05 by the window ending 2023, a lag of about a year relative to Korea, which matches the later and weaker response of Japanese services prices described in Section 2.

The confidence intervals widen as windows include the post-pandemic period, because there are fewer quarters with the new regime. A formal test of the null that the post-2021 slope equals the 2010s slope, based on the interaction coefficient in Table 3, rejects equality in both countries at the 1 per cent level, but the rolling estimates also show that the 95 per cent intervals of the early and late windows overlap for Japan in 2023 and 2024, so we regard the Japanese steepening as more tentative than the Korean one.

subsections.heading: 7.3 Inflation persistence
paragraphs: Table 4 reports persistence, defined as the sum of the coefficients on four lags of regional inflation. In the pooled sample, persistence rises from 0.52 in 2010–2019 to 0.71 in 2021–2024, an increase of 0.19 that is significant at the 1 per cent level and supports H2. The increase is similar in the two countries: from 0.57 to 0.75 in Korea, and from 0.50 to 0.69 in Japan. Persistence increased in all three components of the basket but most for services, for which the sum of coefficients rises from 0.58 to 0.80, whereas for goods other than energy and food it increases from 0.41 to 0.57.

Figure 2 shows the pattern by component. The increase in persistence is economically important: a higher sum of coefficients means that a larger share of any shock to inflation carries over into subsequent quarters, so that the cumulative response to a given shock is substantially larger. Taken together with the steeper curve, the results imply that the post-pandemic regime features both a stronger response of inflation to slack and a slower return to baseline after shocks. The two changes are related: when firms adjust prices more frequently, both the impact response to slack and the pass-through of past inflation into current prices tend to increase [13].

body.heading: 8. Mechanisms and Heterogeneity
paragraphs: What explains the steepening? We examine three channels motivated by the framework: pass-through of energy and food prices into services, the link between slack and wages, and the frequency of price adjustment.

To measure the first channel we construct for each region an index of exposure to energy and food costs: the input-output share of energy and food in the production of local services, interacted with the national change in energy and food prices. We then re-estimate the slope after adding this exposure and its interaction with slack, and compute how much of the post-2021 change in κ disappears. Table 5 reports the decomposition. Across the pooled sample, pass-through of energy and food costs into services accounts for roughly 40 per cent of the steepening. The share is larger in Korea (43 per cent) than in Japan (36 per cent), reflecting both the larger weight of energy-intensive personal services in Korean regional baskets and the larger swing in Korean services prices. This channel is consistent with network models in which sectoral cost shocks propagate through intermediate inputs [24].

The second channel is the wage-price link. Using regional wage data from the monthly labour surveys, we estimate the response of nominal wage growth to slack. The wage Phillips curve is about twice as steep in Korea as in Japan, with a slope of 0.12 in Korea against 0.06 in Japan after 2021, and the relationship between regional wage growth and subsequent services inflation is likewise weaker in Japan. This is consistent with lower wage pass-through in Japan: the spring wage settlements, and the implicit contracts that underpin them [17], dampen the response of wages to local tightness and so limit the translation of tight labour markets into services prices. About 28 per cent of the steepening in the pooled sample is attributable to the wage channel, and the share is larger in Korea. The third channel, price-adjustment frequency, is measured from the share of items in each regional basket whose prices change in a given quarter, which we construct from item-level data for the 12 expenditure groups. The frequency rises by about one-fifth after 2021 and accounts for about 22 per cent of the steepening. The remaining 10 per cent is unexplained.

body.heading: 9. Robustness
paragraphs: Table 6 reports a series of robustness checks on the slope estimates. First, the results do not depend on the slack measure: using the unemployment gap without the vacancy adjustment yields slopes of 0.03 and 0.07 in Korea before and after 2021 and 0.02 and 0.04 in Japan, a smaller but qualitatively similar steepening, and using the vacancy-to-unemployment ratio alone gives essentially the same estimates as the baseline. Second, using headline rather than core inflation produces slopes about a third larger, which is expected given the direct effect of energy and food, but the ratio of post to pre slope is similar.

Third, we vary the instrument. Using the Borusyak et al. approach of relying on the exogeneity of the national shocks rather than the shares gives point estimates within 0.01 of the baseline [12]. Dropping each of the five largest industries from the instrument, one at a time, changes the post-2021 slope by at most 0.01 in either country, which addresses the concern, raised by {11}, that a single industry may drive the results. Fourth, restricting the sample to the largest metropolitan areas, excluding Seoul and Tokyo, or excluding the whole of 2021 does not alter the pattern, and extending the regime break to 2022Q1 produces a similar interaction coefficient. Fifth, allowing the time effects to differ between regions with high and low exposure to the exchange rate leaves the estimates unchanged, suggesting that national expectations are well absorbed. Finally, a sub-sample analysis by region size shows that smaller regions show the same steepening but with larger standard errors.

Table 6 also reports the persistence estimates under alternative lag lengths and under the median-unbiased estimator without the panel correction. The increase of about 0.2 is robust to using two or six lags, and the sum of coefficients before 2021 stays between 0.48 and 0.55.

body.heading: 10. Discussion and Policy Implications
paragraphs: Our results suggest that the Phillips curve in Korea and Japan was meaningfully steeper after 2021 than in the 2010s, and that inflation became more persistent. Several caveats apply to the interpretation. Regional estimates identify the slope for local shocks under common monetary policy, and the slope for national demand shocks may differ [1][2]. If anything, regional estimates tend to understate the aggregate slope because aggregate demand shocks also affect inflation through expectations and exchange rates, which are absorbed by time effects here. At the same time, the steepening that we document may be partly cyclical: very tight labour markets in 2021–2023 may have generated nonlinearity that fades as slack rises [6][26]. Our data cannot yet distinguish a permanent change in the slope from a temporary response to the scale of the shocks.

For monetary policy, the steeper curve has two implications. First, it implies that a given disinflation can be achieved with less slack than in the 2010s. If the slope is 0.09 rather than 0.04 in Korea, then reducing inflation by one percentage point through regional slack alone requires about half as much labour-market loosening, to the extent that the regional slope is informative about the national one. This is the sense in which the sacrifice ratio falls, and it is consistent with the view that recent disinflation has proceeded with less unemployment than earlier experience suggested [23]. Second, the higher persistence implies that the policy response takes longer to pass through, so central banks should expect a slower return to target from any given tightening, and they should be wary of easing prematurely, since a steeper curve implies that inflation responds faster to a renewed tightening of the labour market.

The difference between the two countries carries a separate message. Japan's slope remained about half of Korea's, consistent with lower wage pass-through and a longer experience of low inflation, which anchors expectations at lower levels [17]. For the Bank of Japan, a flatter curve means that inflation is less responsive to labour-market tightness and that reaching sustained 2 per cent inflation depends more on the wage-setting channel than on slack itself, so that continued wage growth in the spring negotiations is crucial. For Korea, in contrast, the steeper curve and the larger role of energy and food pass-through suggest that policy should pay particular attention to second-round effects of commodity shocks on services prices, for which administrative measures such as fuel tax adjustments and utility price controls may buy time but cannot substitute for a monetary response.

The decomposition has implications for the type of shock. Because roughly 40 per cent of the steepening runs through energy and food pass-through, part of the change in slope is not a change in the sensitivity of inflation to domestic slack at all, but a change in how global commodity shocks are transmitted into local prices through intermediate inputs [21][24]. This part may reverse if commodity prices stabilise, and it implies that the steeper curve is partly a state-dependent phenomenon. Our results are therefore consistent with a view in which the post-pandemic regime reflects both large and widespread shocks and a lasting increase in the frequency of price adjustment and the wage-price link, and in which the balance of these two forces will determine how much of the steepening endures.

body.heading: 11. Conclusion
paragraphs: Using city-level and prefecture-level price panels for Korea and Japan, we find that the slope of the regional Phillips curve roughly doubled after 2021, rising from 0.04 to 0.09 in Korea and from 0.02 to 0.05 in Japan, and that the persistence of inflation increased from 0.52 to 0.71. Japan's slope remained about half of Korea's, consistent with lower wage pass-through and a longer experience of low inflation. About 40 per cent of the steepening is attributable to energy and food pass-through into services, with the rest reflecting tighter wage-price links and more frequent price adjustment. Under inflation targeting, disinflation would therefore require less slack than in the 2010s, though the same steeper curve implies a faster inflationary response to renewed tightness.

Several extensions would be valuable. Longer time series will make it possible to test whether the slope reverts as shocks subside. Firm-level price data could separate the frequency of price adjustment from the size of price changes, and linked employer-employee data could clarify the role of wage bargaining institutions in Japan. Comparisons with other regions in the Asia-Pacific that experienced different shocks would help to establish how general the steepening is.

body.heading: Appendix A. Data Construction
paragraphs: Regional prices. Monthly regional consumer price indices are averaged to quarterly frequency. Core regional inflation is the annualised quarterly log change in the index excluding energy and fresh food, rebased to 2020 = 100, with weights from the national expenditure survey held fixed within each base-year revision. Where a base-year revision interrupts a series we splice with the overlapping-quarter growth rate.

Slack. Regional unemployment rates are seasonally adjusted with a regional X-13 filter. The unemployment gap is the deviation from a one-sided Hodrick–Prescott trend with a smoothing parameter of 1,600. The vacancy adjustment is the fitted value from a regression of the gap on the log ratio of job openings to job seekers, estimated separately by country and period.

Instrument. Industry employment shares in 2005 are measured for 19 industry groups. The national growth rate of industry employment is computed excluding the region's own employment, and the national demand shock is the residual of industry exports and public spending from a regression on lagged values. The instrument is standardised by its cross-regional standard deviation in each quarter.

Persistence. Sums of autoregressive coefficients are estimated with four lags of regional inflation and region and quarter fixed effects. The bias correction follows the median-unbiased procedure of Andrews and Chen (1994) adapted to the panel.

title: Emergency Response Times and Cardiac Arrest Survival: Evidence from Seoul's Ambulance Dispatch Reforms
abstract: Rapid emergency response is widely believed to save lives, but causal evidence from outside high-income Western settings is scarce. This paper studies a 2019 reform in Seoul that reallocated ambulance dispatch zones across fire stations, producing exogenous reductions in travel distance for some neighbourhoods but not others. We link 41,200 out-of-hospital cardiac arrest incidents from 2016 to 2023 to dispatch logs and hospital discharge records, and estimate difference-in-differences and instrumental-variable models using the reform-induced change in nearest-station distance as an instrument for response time. The reform shortened response times by 1.8 minutes on average in treated districts. Each additional minute of delay reduces survival to hospital discharge by 1.2 percentage points, and the reform raised survival by 2.1 percentage points, about 14 per cent of the baseline rate. Effects are concentrated in night-time and weekend calls, when stations are thinly staffed, and in older patients. Neurological recovery at discharge improves in parallel. A cost-benefit calculation indicates that the reform generated roughly 3.4 won in avoided health losses per won of operating cost. The findings support investment in dispatch coordination in dense urban settings.

title: School Meals and Learning Outcomes: Evidence from the Expansion of India's PM POSHAN Breakfast Pilots
abstract: India's school meal programme is among the largest in the world, yet little is known about whether adding a second meal improves learning. This paper evaluates the staggered introduction of breakfast alongside the midday meal in primary government schools across 38 districts in four states between 2022 and 2024. Using school-level administrative data on attendance and a panel of 214,000 student assessments from the Annual Status of Education Report and state learning surveys, we compare pilot and non-pilot districts in an event-study framework that accounts for heterogeneous treatment timing. Breakfast raises daily attendance by 2.6 percentage points and mathematics scores by 0.09 standard deviations, with smaller and statistically weaker gains in reading. Effects are two to three times larger for girls from the poorest quintile and in districts with high baseline stunting. Evidence on mechanisms points to reduced short-term hunger rather than improved health, as anthropometric changes over two years are small. Cost per additional student-day of attendance is approximately 11 rupees. We conclude that expanding school feeding at the margin yields measurable learning gains for the most disadvantaged children, with implications for fiscal prioritisation.

title: Social Media, Deposit Runs and Financial Fragility: Evidence from Korea's 2023 Mutual Credit Cooperative Withdrawals
abstract: This paper studies how social media rumours amplified deposit outflows from Korean mutual credit cooperatives during the liquidity scare of late 2022 and early 2023. We assemble daily deposit data for 1,290 branches, geo-coded online posts mentioning cooperative insolvency, and balance-sheet information on delinquency and real-estate exposure. Exploiting variation in the timing of viral posts originating from outside local areas, and controlling for branch fundamentals through fixed effects and a high-dimensional set of balance-sheet interactions, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in rumour intensity raised weekly net outflows by 3.1 percentage points. Importantly, 62 per cent of withdrawn funds were below the statutory insurance limit, which suggests that depositors responded to expected liquidity disruption rather than loss. Branches in areas with higher smartphone use and younger depositors experienced larger outflows. Government liquidity support and a temporary expansion of guarantees halted the run, and roughly 70 per cent of withdrawals returned within two weeks. We interpret the results through a global-games model in which social signals raise common beliefs about strategic withdrawals. The findings underscore the role of information transmission in modern bank fragility.
editorialNote: Deposit outflows at Korean mutual credit cooperatives in early 2023 rose by 3.1 percentage points for each standard-deviation increase in local social media rumour intensity, even for fully insured accounts. Public guarantee announcements reversed roughly 70 per cent of withdrawals within two weeks.

title: Contract Farming and Smallholder Livelihoods: Evidence from Vietnam's Central Highlands Coffee Sector
abstract: Contract farming is promoted as a route for smallholders to access inputs, technical support and premium markets, but selection into contracts complicates evaluation. We use a three-wave household panel of 1,840 coffee-growing households in Dak Lak, Lam Dong and Gia Lai provinces, surveyed in 2018, 2021 and 2024, together with firm-level contract rosters from five exporters. Because exporters expanded sustainability-certified procurement into villages in a staggered sequence driven by proximity to processing plants, we estimate household fixed-effect models with village-level exposure instruments. Contract participation raises net coffee income per hectare by 17 per cent and reduces the coefficient of variation of farm-gate prices faced by 23 per cent, mainly through forward pricing and quality premia. Yields rise by 9 per cent, driven by improved fertiliser and shade-tree management. However, farms below one hectare are 14 percentage points less likely to be offered a contract, and effects for those who participate are small. Female-headed households benefit less from technical training. The results suggest that contract farming can raise incomes but needs complementary measures, such as cooperative aggregation, to include the smallest growers.
editorialNote: Coffee growers on sustainability-certified contracts earned 17 per cent higher net income per hectare and faced 23 per cent lower price risk. Gains were concentrated among farms above one hectare, while the smallest farms were disproportionately excluded.

title: Informal Risk-Sharing Networks after Natural Disasters: Evidence from the 2018 Lombok Earthquakes
abstract: How far do informal risk-sharing networks protect household consumption after a large covariate shock? We study the sequence of earthquakes that struck Lombok, Indonesia, in July and August 2018, using a three-wave panel of 2,300 households surveyed in 2017, 2019 and 2023 with detailed modules on kinship and financial ties, matched to USGS shaking intensity and satellite-based damage proxies. Identification exploits quasi-random variation in peak ground acceleration within villages, conditional on distance to the fault, interacted with pre-quake network size and the diversity of partners' income sources. Strongly shaken households in the top network-size tercile cut consumption by 11 percentage points less than those in the bottom tercile. Network transfers nevertheless covered only 18 per cent of estimated housing damage. The protection shrank by about two thirds where more than half of a household's partners lived in the same village, which confirms the covariate-risk limit of informal sharing. Assets of the best-connected households were rebuilt in three years, against five years for the least connected. Networks smooth consumption but do not insure wealth, and their value depends on how geographically dispersed partners are.

We are grateful to the enumerators and village officials of West and North Lombok who made three rounds of fieldwork possible, and to the Nusa Tenggara Barat provincial disaster agency for sharing damage assessment records. All errors are our own.
dataAvailability: USGS ShakeMap products and the satellite-based damage proxies are publicly available from their providers. The household survey microdata are held by the authors under a confidentiality agreement with the participating villages; de-identified data at the hamlet level, together with replication code, are available from the corresponding author on request.

body.heading: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: When a natural disaster destroys homes, crops and workplaces across a whole community, households in poor countries rarely have formal insurance to fall back on. Private insurance penetration in rural Indonesia is negligible, public disaster assistance is slow and partial, and credit markets are thin. What remains is the web of obligations that links households to their relatives, neighbours and friends. A large literature has shown that such informal arrangements smooth consumption against idiosyncratic shocks such as illness or a poor harvest on a single farm [1][2][7], yet fall well short of full insurance [3][4]. Whether they protect households against shocks that strike everyone at the same time is a different question, and the one with the greatest policy relevance, because covariate shocks are exactly what formal disaster insurance and relief are designed to address.

Theory delivers a sharp prediction. If risk sharing works through bilateral transfers among people who face correlated risks, then the more a shock is shared across the network, the less there is to redistribute [5][6]. A household with many partners who all live in the same hamlet gains little from a big network when the ground shakes under the entire hamlet, whereas a household whose relatives are scattered across islands can draw on partners who were not affected. The size of a network and its geographic and economic diversification are therefore distinct sources of protection, and the empirical literature has rarely been able to separate them, in part because networks are endogenous and large shocks are rare [8][9].

This paper studies a sequence of earthquakes that struck the Indonesian island of Lombok on 29 July, 5 August and 19 August 2018, killing more than 500 people, displacing several hundred thousand and damaging well over 100,000 homes. The shaking was severe but uneven. Because ground motion depends on distance to the rupture, on the depth and composition of local soils and on the direction in which the fault ruptured, households living a few hundred metres apart experienced very different intensities, and thus very different damage. We combine this variation with a three-wave household panel of 2,300 households in 46 villages, interviewed in 2017 (before the earthquakes), in 2019 (one year after) and in 2023 (five years after), in which respondents were asked to name the kin and financial partners with whom they exchange transfers, loans and labour.

Our identification strategy compares households within the same village that experienced different peak ground acceleration (PGA) from the USGS ShakeMap product, conditional on distance to the fault, and asks how the consumption response to strong shaking varies with the size of the household's pre-earthquake network and with the diversity of its partners. The three waves allow us to measure consumption growth between 2017 and 2019 and the recovery of the asset base between 2019 and 2023. Because the networks were mapped in 2017, they are predetermined with respect to the shock, and we show that network size is balanced across exposure to shaking.

We find that networks matter, but less than the literature on idiosyncratic risk might suggest. Among strongly shaken households, consumption fell by 21.4 per cent in the bottom tercile of network size and by 10.4 per cent in the top tercile, a difference of 11 percentage points. Transfers received from network partners, however, averaged only 18 per cent of the estimated cost of housing damage, so most of the loss was absorbed by running down savings, selling assets, borrowing and cutting consumption. The protective effect of a large network falls by about two thirds when more than half of a household's partners live in the same village, and it is amplified when partners' income sources are diversified. Assets were rebuilt to 95 per cent of their pre-earthquake value in a median of three years for the best-connected households and five years for the worst-connected.

We contribute to three literatures. First, we add to the empirical work on risk sharing and covariate shocks, which has mostly studied rainfall and price shocks [3][24][25], by exploiting plausibly exogenous seismic intensity measured at fine spatial resolution and by following households for five years. Second, we contribute to the network literature by measuring both the size and the composition of networks before a shock, building on work that shows how network structure shapes insurance [9][14][15]. Third, we contribute to research on the aftermath of disasters in developing countries, where most existing studies concentrate on aggregate outcomes or on long-run human capital effects [18][19][21]. The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 describes the earthquakes and their aftermath, Section 3 reviews related work, Section 4 sets out a conceptual framework, Sections 5 and 6 describe the data and empirical strategy, Sections 7 to 9 present results, mechanisms and robustness, and Sections 10 and 11 discuss policy implications and conclude.

body.heading: 2. The 2018 Lombok Earthquakes and Their Aftermath
paragraphs: Lombok lies east of Bali in the province of West Nusa Tenggara and is home to roughly 3.5 million people, most of them Sasak Muslims who work in smallholder rice and tobacco farming, fishing, tourism and migrant labour. The island sits directly south of the Flores back-arc thrust, a fault system capable of producing large shallow earthquakes. Between late July and late August 2018 the fault ruptured repeatedly. Table 1 lists the principal events. The first shock on 29 July, of magnitude 6.4, was followed a week later by a magnitude 6.9 event that caused the bulk of the destruction in North and West Lombok, and by two further shocks of magnitude 6.3 and 6.9 on 19 August, which brought additional damage to East Lombok and to areas already weakened.

Official assessments counted more than 500 deaths, hundreds of thousands of displaced people and well over 100,000 damaged homes. Because most rural houses are unreinforced masonry or confined brick of variable quality, damage was strongly related to local ground motion and to building quality rather than to household income alone. Many families lived in tents or temporary shelters for months. The provincial government and the national disaster agency operated a stimulus programme for house reconstruction in which heavily damaged houses were eligible for payments of up to Rp 50 million, with smaller amounts for moderately and lightly damaged houses, but disbursement was slow, required verification of damage and was dispersed over more than two years.

Social organisation on the island is dense. Households belong to extended kin groups, to neighbourhood associations known as banjar or dusun-level groups and to religious and savings groups, and they are linked through the arisan rotating savings associations common in Indonesia. A substantial share of households also have a family member working abroad, particularly in Malaysia and the Gulf, whose remittances arrive through bank and mobile channels. These features make Lombok a natural setting for studying how networks respond when a covariate shock strikes: most partners live nearby, but a meaningful minority live in other villages, other islands or abroad.

body.heading: 3. Related Literature
paragraphs: Our paper builds on the empirical literature on consumption insurance. Townsend {1} and Cochrane {3} test whether household consumption co-moves with idiosyncratic income once aggregate resources are controlled for, and Mace {4} shows the same logic applied to the United States. Udry {2} documents state-contingent loans among Nigerian villagers, while Fafchamps and Lund {7} find that gifts and informal loans in the Philippines respond to illness and unemployment shocks but not to the covariate component of income. A theoretical branch, represented by Coate and Ravallion {5} and Ligon, Thomas and Worrall {6}, explains incomplete insurance through limited commitment: transfers must be self-enforcing, so they cannot exceed what each party would be willing to give in return for future support. Rosenzweig and Stark {27} show that marriage across villages in India works as a device for spreading risk spatially, and Gertler and Gruber {28} find that Indonesian households insure only part of the consumption cost of serious illness, which anticipates the limits we document for disasters.

A second literature turns to networks. Fafchamps and Gubert {8} show that geographic proximity and kinship predict the formation of risk-sharing links, and Ambrus, Mobius and Szeidl {9} characterise when networks can support efficient transfers and how the pattern of links determines consumption risk. Jackson, Rodriguez-Barraquer and Tan {14} argue that favour exchange sustains itself through social quilts of overlapping triangles, and Genicot and Ray {15} study how groups of different sizes form and dissolve. On the empirical side, Kinnan and Townsend {12} link kinship and financial networks to risk reduction in Thailand, Karlan and co-authors {13} show that social collateral supports lending, and Jack and Suri {10} demonstrate that cheaper transfers through M-PESA increased risk sharing in Kenya. Blumenstock, Eagle and Fafchamps {11} find that, after earthquakes in Rwanda, airtime transfers flow from the unaffected to the affected, which is evidence that networks can channel help in the aftermath of a disaster, but that flows are small relative to the losses.

A third strand studies disasters themselves. Cameron and Shah {16} find that earthquake and flood victims in Indonesia become more risk averse, and Cassar, Healy and von Kessler {17} document changes in trust and risk preferences after the Thai tsunami. Gignoux and Menéndez {18} follow households for fifteen years after earthquakes in Indonesia and find that short-run losses give way to long-run gains in welfare as reconstruction and migration proceed. Kahn {19}, Strömberg {20} and Noy {21} document that disaster mortality and macroeconomic costs vary strongly with income and institutions, and Skoufias {22} and Carter and co-authors {23} analyse coping strategies, including asset sales, that can lock households into poverty traps. Deryugina {26} shows for the United States that hurricane losses are cushioned mainly through public transfers rather than private insurance. We add direct evidence on how the structure of informal networks mediates consumption and asset dynamics when the shock hits an entire community.

body.heading: 4. Conceptual Framework
paragraphs: We formalise the intuition with a stylised model of bilateral transfers. Household i belongs to a network of partners N_i and suffers a loss L_i from the earthquake. Under limited commitment, partner j is willing to transfer t_ij to i only if the net present value of continuing the relationship exceeds the gain from defaulting. Partners who are not themselves hit by the shock have high marginal utility of consumption in a normal state and can afford to transfer; partners who are hit have a high marginal utility and transfer little or demand help in return. The transfers that household i can expect are therefore increasing in the number of partners and in the share of them who are unaffected, and they are bounded above by what the partners' own budget constraints allow [9][14].

Three predictions follow. First, holding the severity of the shock fixed, consumption should fall less for households with larger networks (network size effect). Second, the protection afforded by a given network should be smaller if the partners are more exposed to the same shock, which happens when they live in the same village (covariate-risk limit). Third, protection should be greater when partners derive income from diverse sources, because their capacity to give is less correlated with that of the household and with each other (income diversification). In addition, because informal transfers are typically small and are repaid or reciprocated over time, they are more likely to smooth consumption than to rebuild the asset base, so networks may speed recovery by easing the need for distress sales of productive assets [23][31]. We take these predictions to the data in turn.

body.heading: 5. Data
paragraphs: Our analysis combines a purpose-built household panel with physical measures of earthquake intensity and damage. This section describes each component and the construction of the network measures.

subsections.heading: 5.1 The household survey
paragraphs: We use a three-wave panel of households in 46 villages across the districts of West, North and Central Lombok. The first wave was fielded between May and July 2017, before the earthquakes, as part of a baseline survey on household finance and village institutions; the villages were chosen to span the range of kinship density and distance from the Flores back-arc thrust, and 10 households were sampled in each of 230 hamlets (dusun). The second wave was fielded in September and October 2019 and the third in the same months of 2023. Of the 2,527 households interviewed in 2017, 2,300 (91 per cent) were interviewed in all three waves, and we restrict attention to this balanced panel. Attrition is unrelated to shaking intensity, to network size or to the interaction of the two (Appendix A).

Consumption is measured with a recall module covering 38 food items over the previous week and 24 non-food items over the previous month and year, expressed in per capita monthly rupiah at 2017 prices. The asset index aggregates housing quality, productive assets, livestock and durables using 2017 market prices and is normalised so that the 2017 value for each household equals 100. A retrospective module in 2023 records the date at which each household completed reconstruction of its house and replacement of lost productive assets, which we use to construct recovery times. Housing damage is estimated as the cost of repairing or rebuilding damaged structures to their pre-earthquake quality, using a damage-grade assessment by trained enumerators and local unit costs.

subsections.heading: 5.2 Network measures
paragraphs: In 2017 each respondent was asked to name, up to a limit of 25, the people outside the household who had given or received money, food or labour during the past year, or who would be asked for a loan of one month's household expenditure in an emergency. The respondent also reported the relationship (kin or non-kin), the partner's village and the partner's main source of income. We follow the approach of Banerjee and co-authors {30} in eliciting names from self-reports and confirmed links with partners who were themselves in the survey. Network size is the number of partners named; we classify households into terciles (3 or fewer, 4 to 9 and 10 or more partners) and also use the standardised logarithm. The same-village share is the fraction of partners who live in the household's village, and partner income diversity is one minus the Herfindahl index of the partners' main income sources (farming, trade, wage work, migration and remittances, and public employment).

subsections.heading: 5.3 Shaking intensity and damage proxies
paragraphs: We obtain PGA, expressed as a fraction of gravitational acceleration (g), from the USGS ShakeMap products for the four main events, which combine ground-motion prediction equations with seismometer records and site amplification derived from the topographic slope-based Vs30 proxy. We take the maximum PGA over the sequence at the hamlet's coordinates on a roughly one-kilometre grid. We classify a household as strongly shaken if the hamlet's PGA exceeded 0.25 g, a level at which unreinforced masonry typically suffers heavy damage, and we also use continuous PGA in robustness analysis. We supplement the survey with satellite-based damage proxies from the Copernicus damage grading maps and building-footprint change detection, aggregated to the hamlet. These proxies are used to validate the ShakeMap exposure measure, and the hamlet-level correlation between PGA and the satellite damage share is 0.64.

body.heading: 6. Empirical Strategy
paragraphs: Our empirical strategy asks how the consumption response to shaking depends on pre-earthquake networks, and exploits the fact that the intensity of ground motion varies within villages for reasons that households did not choose.

subsections.heading: 6.1 Specification
paragraphs: Our baseline specification is a long difference between the 2017 and 2019 waves. For household i in hamlet h of village v, the change in log per capita consumption is regressed on an indicator for strong shaking, on its interaction with the household's network tercile, on village fixed effects and on controls: Δ ln C_ihv = α_v + β S_h + γ_M (S_h × Middle_i) + γ_T (S_h × Top_i) + δ′X_i + φ ln Dist_h + ε_ihv, where S_h indicates PGA above 0.25 g, Middle_i and Top_i indicate the network terciles, X_i includes baseline consumption, household size, education and income composition together with the main effects of the terciles, and Dist_h is distance to the nearest fault trace. The coefficient β is the effect of strong shaking on households in the bottom tercile, and γ_T measures how much smaller the loss is for the top tercile. We cluster standard errors at the village level and report Conley standard errors with a 10-kilometre cutoff to allow for spatial correlation [29].

subsections.heading: 6.2 Identification
paragraphs: The identifying assumption is that conditional on village fixed effects and on distance to the fault, strong shaking is unrelated to household characteristics that also influence the evolution of consumption, including network size. Ground motion depends on local geology, on site amplification and on rupture directivity, which are not chosen by households; and because the hamlet is the unit at which exposure varies, we are comparing hamlets within villages that happened to be placed on softer or firmer ground. Table 2 shows that mean PGA, the incidence of strong shaking and distance to the fault do not differ across network terciles, and that the main differences between terciles are in schooling, income composition and baseline consumption. We control for these and show in Section 9 that interacting shaking with the full set of baseline characteristics leaves the results unchanged.

A second concern is that network size is itself correlated with unobserved characteristics such as entrepreneurial ability or trust, which might independently determine the consumption response. Two features of the design address this. The network was measured before the shock, so it cannot respond to damage, and we show in Section 9 that within-village variation in network size that is orthogonal to observables, constructed using the number of siblings and the household head's birth order as instruments, yields similar interaction effects. We also report placebo tests in which the 2017 networks interact with shaking in a pre-period for which we have retrospective consumption data. Figure 1 plots the consumption change by bins of PGA for the bottom and top terciles and shows that the gap opens only at high intensities, a pattern that is hard to attribute to unobserved differences that would operate at all levels of exposure.

body.heading: 7. Results
paragraphs: We present three sets of results: the consumption response and its dependence on network size, the transfers that explain it, and the limits that arise when partners are exposed to the same shock.

subsections.heading: 7.1 Consumption response
paragraphs: Table 3 reports the effect of strong shaking on the change in log consumption between 2017 and 2019. Column 1 shows that, on average, strongly shaken households reduced consumption by 15.5 per cent relative to households in less shaken parts of the same village, an effect that is large relative to typical consumption volatility in the sample. Column 2 interacts shaking with the standardised log of network size and shows that a one standard deviation increase in network size reduces the loss by 4.9 percentage points. Column 3 uses terciles. In the bottom tercile, strong shaking lowers consumption by 21.4 per cent; the loss is 6.3 percentage points smaller in the middle tercile and 11.0 percentage points smaller in the top tercile, so that the strongly shaken households with the largest networks reduced consumption by about 10.4 per cent.

The estimated protection is economically significant, but it is partial. Even in the top tercile, a loss of 10 per cent of consumption for at least a year is a considerable hardship for households that were near the national poverty line before the earthquakes, and in the bottom tercile the loss approaches a quarter of consumption. Column 4 adds the diversity of partners' income sources: a one standard deviation increase in diversity reduces the loss by a further 4.2 percentage points and lowers the tercile interaction to 9.7, so some of the benefit of large networks operates through the fact that bigger networks contain more diverse partners. Column 5 adds household controls and hamlet-level damage proxies and returns an estimate of 10.7 for the top tercile, close to the baseline.

subsections.heading: 7.2 Transfers and coping
paragraphs: Table 4 examines the transfers that underlie these results among strongly shaken households. Households in the top tercile received Rp 9.6 million from their networks on average, against Rp 4.1 million in the bottom tercile, while the mean estimated housing damage was the same, at about Rp 38.6 million. Network transfers therefore covered 24.8 per cent of damage in the top tercile and 10.7 per cent in the bottom tercile, and 18 per cent overall. The composition of the transfers also differs. In the bottom tercile, the great majority of support came from partners in the same village, who were themselves affected and could give little, whereas in the top tercile roughly 41 per cent came from partners outside the village, mostly relatives working elsewhere in Indonesia or abroad.

Government housing assistance was similar across terciles, at Rp 8.9 million on average, suggesting that targeting did not systematically favour connected or unconnected households. Taken together, transfers from networks and the state covered about 41 per cent of damage. The remainder fell on households, which responded by drawing down savings, borrowing, selling livestock and gold, and cutting consumption. These patterns echo the finding that informal risk sharing is limited in what it can cover after covariate shocks [3][5], and they are broadly consistent with the finding of limited airtime flows after disasters in Rwanda [11].

subsections.heading: 7.3 The covariate-risk limit
paragraphs: The central theoretical prediction is that networks protect less when partners are exposed to the same shock. Table 5 splits the sample by the 2017 share of partners residing in the household's village. In Panel A, which contains the 62 per cent of households with at most half their partners in the village, strong shaking reduces consumption by 23.1 per cent in the bottom tercile and the top tercile is protected by 14.8 percentage points. In Panel B, the 38 per cent of households with more than half of their partners in the village, the corresponding protection is only 4.9 percentage points. The difference of 9.9 points, shown in column 3, represents a decline in insurance of about two thirds and is statistically significant at the 5 per cent level.

Column 4 asks whether partner diversity operates independently of location. A one standard deviation increase in partners' income diversity raises protection among the top tercile by a further 7.1 percentage points, even after allowing for the same-village share. The two margins are thus complementary: what matters is not how many people a household can call on, but how many of them are free of the shock and have a different source of income. This is consistent with models in which transfer capacity depends on the correlation of partners' consumption with the household's [9][14], and it helps to explain why large but local networks were of limited help in the most affected hamlets.

body.heading: 8. Mechanisms and Heterogeneity
paragraphs: The previous section identifies the main insurance role of networks; here we examine how long it lasts and who benefits most. We use the 2023 wave and the retrospective module to study the recovery of assets, which captures a margin that consumption smoothing alone does not.

Table 6 reports the evolution of the asset index for strongly shaken households. In 2019, one year after the earthquakes, the asset index of these households stood at 59 per cent of its 2017 value in the bottom tercile, 67 per cent in the middle tercile and 74 per cent in the top tercile; by 2023 the corresponding figures were 94, 101 and 107 per cent. The median time to restore assets to 95 per cent of the pre-earthquake level, based on the retrospective reconstruction dates, was five years in the bottom tercile, four in the middle and three in the top tercile. Figure 2 presents the same comparison graphically. Well-connected households were not only better protected in consumption; they rebuilt faster, with a lower probability of distress sales (Table 4) and a smaller recourse to moneylenders.

Two mechanisms are consistent with this pattern. First, connected households faced less pressure to liquidate productive assets at depressed prices, which preserved their capacity to generate income and is consistent with the asset-based poverty trap logic of Carter and Barrett [31] and with the evidence that disasters can set back asset accumulation [23]. Second, connected households obtained more labour and in-kind help for reconstruction from partners outside the village. We find that the contribution of outside partners is larger in the top tercile, which suggests that diversification is valuable in the recovery phase as well as in the initial response. The protective effect of networks is also larger for households headed by women and for those with a main income from farming, groups for which formal safety nets are weakest, though the differences are imprecise.

body.heading: 9. Robustness
paragraphs: We subject the central result to several checks, summarised here. First, using continuous PGA in place of the indicator for strong shaking, the interaction between PGA (standardised) and the top network tercile is 0.041 (standard error 0.014), and the results are similar when the threshold is moved to 0.20 g or 0.30 g, where the top-tercile protection ranges from 9.2 to 12.1 percentage points. Replacing ShakeMap exposure with the satellite-based damage share of the hamlet delivers a top-tercile interaction of 0.096.

Second, we address the endogeneity of networks. Instrumenting network size with the number of living siblings and the household head's birth order, the first-stage F-statistic is 24 and the second-stage interaction is 0.128 (standard error 0.058), somewhat larger than the baseline and consistent with attenuation of the ordinary least squares estimates because of measurement error in networks. A placebo test that interacts shaking with network size in retrospective consumption growth between 2015 and 2017 yields coefficients close to zero. Interacting shaking with the complete set of baseline controls changes the main estimate by less than 0.01.

Third, we study attrition and spatial dependence. Inverse probability weights for attrition between 2017 and 2019 leave the results unchanged, and so does the exclusion of the 12 hamlets for which damage assessments were incomplete. Conley standard errors with 10-kilometre and 25-kilometre cutoffs [29] increase the standard error of the top-tercile interaction from 0.032 to 0.037 and 0.041, and the estimate remains significant at the 1 and 5 per cent levels respectively. Finally, the results do not depend on how networks are measured: restricting the network to kin, to partners who were also interviewed or to partners with whom reciprocal flows were reported, the top-tercile protection varies between 8.4 and 12.3 percentage points.

body.heading: 10. Discussion and Policy Implications
paragraphs: Our results support a nuanced view of informal insurance. On the one hand, networks matter: strongly shaken households with large networks suffered a consumption loss about half the size of those with few partners, and they rebuilt their asset base two years faster. On the other hand, informal transfers covered less than a fifth of the damage, and the protection nearly vanished when partners shared the household's location. Informal insurance can smooth consumption against moderate losses but cannot substitute for formal mechanisms in the face of a large covariate shock [25][26].

Three policy implications follow. First, because most informal help comes from nearby, disaster financing should be designed with the geography of networks in mind. Cash transfers delivered quickly to affected hamlets can relieve the constraint on partners who might otherwise be unable to give. Programmes that complement informal transfers, for example by matching them or by speeding verification of damage, could increase the pass-through of outside help. Second, ex ante instruments that pool risk across space, such as national catastrophe insurance, index insurance and public reconstruction funds, are most valuable where networks are geographically concentrated. Households who lack connected partners elsewhere are the ones who benefit most from them. Third, policies that facilitate cheap, secure transfers between affected and unaffected areas, including mobile money and remittance channels [10][11], can reinforce informal sharing by making it easier for dispersed partners to help.

Several limitations should be noted. Our identification relies on conditional variation in ground motion within villages, and although the balance evidence is reassuring we cannot rule out that unobserved differences interact with shaking. We measure networks through the lens of the respondent and may miss weaker ties that matter in emergencies. The consumption response is measured one year after the earthquakes, and we cannot observe the full path of consumption in the first months. Finally, Lombok is a Muslim-majority island with dense kin groups and active religious charity, so the patterns may not transfer to settings where informal ties are weaker. The longer horizon of the panel, which spans five years, is a strength, but our estimates apply to a single disaster sequence.

body.heading: 11. Conclusion
paragraphs: Using three rounds of survey data and quasi-random variation in earthquake shaking within villages, we show that informal risk-sharing networks provide real but limited protection after a large covariate shock. Households in the top network tercile cut consumption by 11 percentage points less than those in the bottom tercile, yet transfers covered only 18 per cent of the damage and recovery of assets took five years for the least connected households against three for the best connected. When more than half of a household's partners lived in the same village, the protective effect fell by about two thirds.

These findings imply that policy cannot rely on informal arrangements to cushion communities against shocks that strike everyone at once, and that the design of disaster relief should take into account the spatial structure of social networks. Future work should examine how the mix between informal and formal support evolves as financial inclusion deepens, whether networks reorganise toward more dispersed partners after a disaster, and whether the cost of transfers to partners, in terms of their own consumption and investment, offsets some of the benefits we document.

body.heading: Appendix A. Data Construction and Attrition
paragraphs: Network elicitation. In 2017 respondents were first asked an open name generator on gifts, loans and labour exchange in the past year and then a hypothetical question about whom they would approach for a loan equal to one month of household expenditure. Names were matched to survey households using village rosters, and partners were coded as kin if the respondent reported a blood or marriage relationship. Network size is capped at 25, which binds for 1.4 per cent of households.

Shaking and damage. ShakeMap PGA is taken at the centroid of the hamlet's surveyed households and the maximum over the four main events is retained. Housing damage in rupiah is the sum of repair costs for each structure, graded from 0 to 4, using the unit costs reported in the 2019 wave for rebuilding comparable structures. Satellite damage shares are the proportion of building footprints within 500 metres of the hamlet centroid classified as damaged or destroyed.

Attrition. Of the 2,527 households interviewed in 2017, 227 were not found in at least one later wave; the main reasons were permanent relocation after the earthquakes (41 per cent) and refusals. A regression of attrition on strong shaking, network tercile and their interaction yields coefficients that are individually and jointly insignificant (p = 0.44). Inverse-probability weighting does not change any of the results.

title: Entry, Pricing and Consumer Welfare in Mobile Data Markets: Evidence from Reliance Jio's Launch in India

authors.name: Siddharth Mukherjee
authors.department: Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research

abstract: This paper analyses how the 2016 entry of a low-price, fourth-generation operator reshaped competition and consumer welfare in India's mobile data market. We combine regulator data on quarterly subscribers, usage and revenue by telecom circle with 3.2 million plan-level price observations from 2015 to 2022. Using staggered rollout of network coverage across 22 circles as quasi-experimental variation, we estimate that entry cut the effective price per gigabyte by 91 per cent and raised monthly data consumption per subscriber from 0.3 to 2.4 gigabytes. Incumbent operators responded with bundled plans and exit through consolidation, reducing the number of private operators from eight to three by 2021. We estimate a nested-logit demand system with plan characteristics and recover markups and consumer surplus. Entry increased annual consumer surplus per subscriber by an amount equal to about 12 per cent of household telecom spending, with larger gains in rural circles where prior data use was minimal. Counterfactual simulations show that post-consolidation markups rose by 9 per cent relative to the peak-competition period, partially eroding earlier welfare gains. We discuss the implications for merger review in emerging-market telecommunications.
editorialNote: After Jio's 2016 entry, the effective price per gigabyte of mobile data fell by 91 per cent and monthly data use per subscriber rose nearly eightfold. Estimated consumer surplus gains were about 12 per cent of annual household telecommunication spending, with larger gains in rural circles.

title: Treaty Ports and the Long-Run Geography of Industry in China
abstract: This paper revisits the long-run effects of the Chinese treaty ports opened to foreign trade after 1842 on the spatial distribution of industry. We construct a prefecture-level dataset linking historical records on port openings, early modern railway lines and treaty-era factories to modern economic census data from 2004 to 2018. To address endogenous port selection, we exploit a set of ports designated through treaty negotiations whose locations were determined by pre-existing naval geography and river navigability, comparing them with prefectures that were shortlisted but not opened. Treaty-port prefectures have a manufacturing employment share 22 per cent higher than comparable prefectures, and 1.9 times the density of firms in export-intensive industries. A mediation analysis shows that about 75 per cent of the persistent gap operates through market-access advantages from historical trade links and railway connections, whereas contemporary institutional quality and human capital account for less than a fifth. Effects decline with distance from the port and disappear beyond roughly 150 kilometres. The results favour a path-dependent agglomeration interpretation over an institutional-legacy one, and caution against generalising colonial-era effects across settings.

title: Time-of-Use Pricing and Residential Peak Demand: Smart-Meter Evidence from Japan
abstract: As electricity systems integrate variable renewable energy, shaping household demand through time-varying prices is a central policy question. This paper evaluates the response of residential consumers to time-of-use tariffs using half-hourly smart-meter data from 640,000 households served by two regional utilities in Japan between 2019 and 2024. Customers could opt into the tariff, but a billing-system migration moved some customers by default on dates unrelated to their consumption, providing quasi-random variation which we exploit with an event-study design. Evening peak consumption (5 to 9 pm) falls by 8.7 per cent after the switch, implying an own-price elasticity of -0.14 during peak hours, while off-peak consumption rises by 3.2 per cent. Overall electricity use is unchanged. Responses are about twice as large among households with automated appliances and those with rooftop solar and batteries, and increase over the first year as households learn. We estimate that scaling the tariff to the whole service area would lower peak capacity needs by 3.9 per cent, saving roughly 41 billion yen in capacity costs per year. Distributional analysis shows that low-income households gain on average.

title: Testing for Real Exchange Rate Mean Reversion in Asia: Panel Unit Root Tests with Cross-Sectional Dependence and Structural Breaks
abstract: Whether real exchange rates revert to purchasing power parity is a long-standing question with direct implications for competitiveness assessments in emerging Asia. This paper examines mean reversion in the real exchange rates of 14 Asian economies against the US dollar using monthly data from 1995 to 2024. We show through Monte Carlo simulations that first-generation panel unit root tests suffer from substantial size distortion when cross-sectional dependence is generated by global dollar cycles, rejecting a true unit root in up to 42 per cent of replications at the nominal 5 per cent level. We propose a simple procedure that filters common factors using cross-sectional averages and allows for a single endogenously estimated structural break in each series. Applying the procedure, the rejection frequency of the unit root null falls from 71 per cent under conventional tests to 38 per cent, and the break-corrected half-life of deviations is 2.9 years, compared with 4.6 years when breaks are ignored. Evidence of mean reversion is stronger for economies with managed floats than for freely floating currencies. The results suggest that earlier support for relative PPP in Asia partly reflects methodological artefacts, and that long-run misalignment assessments should use factor-augmented tests.
